Accelerating AI compute satellite engineering with an AI agent and GPU simulation
Author: <author> assisted by AI agent <assistant>
Engineers set the requirements. An AI agent runs the analysis. Physics solvers check the selected design.
Human requirements /
design decisions
AI agent (closed source)
Open analysis scripts
Apache-2.0
GPU: Warp, PhysicsNeMo, Newton
CPU: CalculiX FEA
Solver checks
Human review /
approval
Full repo (GitHub)
PROBLEM
Putting AI data centers in orbit can ease power generation
concerns on Earth, but the satellites must be mass- and
volume-efficient to meet launch and radiative cooling needs.
SpaceX's published targets of 250 kW peak per satellite and 75
kW per ton imply 30 satellites × 250 kW = 7.5 MW installed
peak per 100 t Starship launch. An engineer and an AI agent
explored the design space and selected a high-level
architecture to meet that target.
Source: spacex.com/spacexai/starmind
DESIGN ARCHITECTURE (PER SATELLITE)
Compute:
one Vera Rubin NVL72 (72 GPUs + 36 CPUs); 250
kW peak at beginning of life. Assumed 640.38 kg payload
allocation in a 600 × 1200 × 937 mm box.
Mass:
3,026 kg per satellite; all 30 satellites fit one 100 t
Starship at 90.8 t, leaving 2 t for the dispenser and a 7.2 t
reserve.
Power:
862 m² solar array; assumed module rating 324.55
W/m² on its remaining planar area; 175 kW nominal in sunlight
and a 164.4 kW annual average, including eclipse.
Thermal:
Rubin GPU/HBM ≈370 K nominal target (est.
371–373 K), higher in edge cases; junction temperatures not
yet qualified. Coolant inlet peaks at 392 K. 140 radiator
panels; coating emissivity 0.92. Fins and tubes selected by
search; modeled glycol-water loop.
Rack structure:
Compute rack screening (CalculiX beam
model, 6 g axial / 2 g lateral, FS 1.25): a ≈50 kg aluminum
frame inside the 640 kg allocation reaches 35 Hz (Falcon
reference) with large strength margins.
Panel vibration:
Stowed radiator-panel first mode 128–153
Hz across support-pad assumptions (≈139 Hz nominal), well
above the 35 Hz reference.
Folding and deployment:
31/31 representative hinge locks
latch in Newton rigid simulation; sampled clearance passes.
A basis for further detailed design. Simulation study, not flight
qualification.
Illustrative Isaac Sim RTX render, not flight validation. Earth:
NASA Blue Marble.
1  What did the search find? | Warp
1.81M designs; 3,048 feasible, lightest picked
Screening candidates (color: panels)
Stress scenarios
Only 41.66% of assumed scenarios meet the 393 K coolant cap.
1.05M coating / power / sun-exposure scenarios; not flight reliability.
Star: screening estimate. Diamond: solver re-check, 3026.21 kg / 140 panels.
2  What ran faster? | GB10 benchmark
32.9× faster than one GB10 CPU core
0.214 s
7.02 s
Same fp64 workload; warm kernel only; median of 3 runs. Warp 1.18.0.
1,806,336 combinations; CPU: 1 Cortex-X925 core / 1 thread.
Device-synchronized timer; setup/JIT/readback excluded.
8.46M designs/s; input SHA256 94e1b3ae978b… (full hash in repo).
3  Can we trust the search? | PhysicsNeMo / Tape
Max |Δη| = 9.3e-5 (held out)
PhysicsNeMo: 384 training / 128 held-out labels; η = fin efficiency.
Selected fins re-solved with Warp; approximation is not flight validation.
warp.Tape: 0.65% relaxed mass gap; gradient check passed.
Continuous relaxation, not adopted hardware or a global optimum.
4  Does it deploy? | Newton / Warp
31 / 31 modeled hinge locks
Rigid panels / fixed bus; representative hinges, not full flight tests.
Independent sampled-clearance check passed; angle parity 0.0061°.
Newton 1.7.0 and Warp 1.18.0 on CUDA; agreement is not hardware validation.
Flexible hardware and force-step convergence remain open.
≈11 days recorded span | ≥44.1 h GB10 computer-job time* | Why it matters: more checks before hardware, not just a faster kernel
*CPU + GPU jobs, including rendering; not GPU-hours. Start: earliest-retained-input timestamp proxy, not verified first problem definition.
